p.title: An Improved D* Lite-Based Dynamic Route Planning Algorithm for Ships in Arctic Waters
p.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering, 12, 2323 (MDPI)

ext.title: An Improved D* Lite-Based Dynamic Route Planning Algorithm for Ships in Arctic Waters
ext.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering, 12, 2323 (MDPI, Basel); published 18 Dec 2024
ext.document_type: Journal article: algorithm design plus simulation benchmark (open access, CC BY 4.0)
ext.coverage: Full text read (all 1,126 extracted lines, pp. 1-22, including references and disclaimer). Metadata hint confirmed: title, year, venue, DOI correct. No Paul markup files were supplied (task listed none). Topical fit to the vault is low: the paper covers graph-search path planning only. It has no content on lobbying, elections, turnout, persuasion, legislators, text measurement, or social networks, beyond the general fact that the graph is a grid.
ext.research_question: How can D* Lite dynamic replanning be made cheap enough for real-time ship routing in Arctic waters, where ice conditions change over large areas, while keeping route distance and average risk close to full re-planning? The authors set the goal as cutting node updates and planning time without changing the heuristic.
ext.theory: No social-science theory. The basis is graph-search path planning: incremental replanning from LPA* and D* (Koenig and Likhachev 2002, ref. 26), a risk-weighted movement cost (cost = delta*r + d, Eq. 12), and a ship-specific icebreaking limit (maximum continuous ice-breaking thickness) used in place of ice-class rules.
ext.data: Sea ice thickness and related ice data from CryoSat-2 (European Space Agency), stated in Sec. 4 (data availability: NSIDC, accessed 29 April 2024). Study area 55-90 degrees N, grid 448 x 304 cells at 25 km x 25 km. Unit: grid cell (node) and route update. Two simulated voyages, one per period: freezing (October 2023 dataset, 26 route updates) and melting (mid-April to mid-May 2023, 24 route updates). No ship sample. Ship parameters are a single hypothetical vessel with icebreaking thickness 1.2 m (freezing) or 2.8 m (melting), risk threshold 1, and a fixed update distance of 8 grid units per update. Text says this is "approximately 432 nautical miles", which does not match the stated grid resolution (see limitations).
ext.scope: Population: one Arctic region, two ice periods (freezing October 2023; melting April-May 2023), one ship type parameterized by icebreaking thickness and safety coefficient. Institution: Shanghai Maritime University (Merchant Marine College). Era: 2023 ice data, paper published Dec 2024. Speed differences by ice condition are excluded (Sec. 4, p. 13).
ext.method: Improved D* Lite with three modified rules. (1) Local update (Sec. 2.2, Eq. 5, Algorithm 1): a node that becomes an obstacle takes its cost from the old data, and a node that becomes navigable takes its cost from the new data, so updates do not spread through the whole map. (2) Path extraction (Sec. 2.3, Eq. 6, Algorithm 2): the next node is the unexplored successor minimizing c + g, which avoids deadlocks at the boundary of updated regions. (3) Path optimization (Sec. 2.4, Eqs. 7-9): shortcut any segment where the direct connection costs less and has no obstacles. Risk r = h x C / Icemax (Eq. 10); cost = delta*r + d (Eq. 12); average route risk R = sum(r_i d_i)/sum(d_i) (Eq. 13). Non-navigable cells are land, cells with average ice thickness above Icemax, and cells with r above the threshold (Sec. 3.1). Benchmarks: global re-planning every update, and the original D* Lite. All three run on identical ice snapshots and ship positions.
ext.identification_strategy: None. This is a simulation benchmark, not a causal design. Validity rests on comparing against global re-planning, treated as optimal under the same heuristic (Sec. 4.1, p. 14-15), and against the original D* Lite. Parameter effects (Icemax, delta) are shown only by re-running the same voyage with different settings (Sec. 4.3, Table 5).

key_findings.finding: Freezing period, improved vs original D* Lite: nodes updated fell by 34.9% (18,468 vs 28,351); planning time fell by 46.2% (924 s vs 1,720 s). Voyage distance 2,558.7 vs 2,561.4 n mi; average risk identical at 0.076.
Freezing period, improved vs global re-planning: nodes updated fell 74.6% and planning time fell 72.7%. Route quality matched global re-planning on risk, with distance within about 0.1%.
Melting period, improved vs original D* Lite: nodes updated fell 79.5% and planning time fell 85.7%. Voyage distance 2,419.1 vs 2,418.1 n mi; risk identical at 0.615.
Melting period, improved vs global re-planning: nodes updated fell 85.3% and planning time fell 86.7%.

Sensitivity, freezing period: raising Icemax from 1.0 to 1.4 m shortens the route (2,654.5 to 2,459.9 n mi) and raises average risk (0.002 to 0.113). Raising delta from 1 to 3 at 1.2 m lengthens the route (2,558.7 to 2,645.5 n mi) and lowers risk (0.076 to 0.039).

Sensitivity, melting period: delta 1 to 3 at 2.8 m lengthens the route (2,419.1 to 2,644.1 n mi) and lowers risk (0.615 to 0.468). Risk does not fall monotonically with Icemax: at delta 1 it is 0.625, 0.631, 0.615 for 2.4, 2.6, 2.8 m.
Safety coefficient delta = 3 is adopted as sufficient on the basis of unpublished simulations: higher values did not change route outcomes much.

Discussion, single illustrative map (Icemax 0.8 m, PC-6-equivalent): the POLARIS-based route crosses non-navigable cells, while the proposed risk formula routes around them. Qualitative only, no numbers.
Conclusion claims planning-efficiency gains are directly proportional to ice-data completeness. Only two periods were tested, so this is an untested claim.

measures: Total voyage distance (n mi), summed over the route
Average route risk R = sum(r_i d_i)/sum(d_i) (Eq. 13)
Cell risk r = h x C / Icemax (Eq. 10), where h is average ice thickness, C is ice density, Icemax is maximum continuous icebreaking thickness
Planning time (s) per full dynamic run
Number of nodes updated per run
Movement cost cost = delta*r + d (Eq. 12); d is 1 or 0.707 for 8-neighbour moves
limitations: Authors: ship speed varies with ice and is not modelled; the update distance is fixed at 8 grid units per update (Sec. 4, p. 13).
Authors: forecast uncertainty and floating-ice drift can make a route invalid, so local obstacle avoidance is future work (Sec. 5, p. 20).
Authors: POLARIS was not used because it works from ice type and ice class, not thickness and maximum icebreaking thickness (Sec. 5, p. 19).
Authors: ice thickness data are unreliable in rapidly changing months, and no average-thickness data were released June-September, so only two windows were studied (Sec. 4, p. 13).
Mine: one simulated voyage per period with no repetition, variance, or confidence intervals; timing claims rest on single runs.
Mine: no hardware or software specification is given for the timings in Tables 3-4.
Mine: the text's 0.07% voyage/risk error figures do not reproduce from Tables 3-4 (voyage deviation is 0.10% freezing vs original and 0.04% melting vs original; risk is identical).
Mine: the text says 8 grid units equal about 432 n mi, but 8 x 25 km = 200 km, about 108 n mi.
Mine: the text says risk rises with Icemax, but in the melting sweep at delta 1 risk goes 0.625, 0.631, 0.615, which is not monotone.
Mine: the conclusion's proportionality claim about ice-data completeness rests on two periods only.
Mine: the abstract's 'gradual and convergent' ice-change premise is asserted, not tested.

rel.summary_md:
Xu et al. (2024) change D* Lite so that a ship's route can be re-planned cheaply as Arctic ice changes. The test grid is 448 x 304 cells at 25 km. They make three changes: (1) a local-update rule, where a cell that becomes blocked keeps its old cost and a cell that opens takes its new cost, so changes don't spread across the whole map; (2) a path-extraction rule that picks the unexplored successor with the lowest c+g, which avoids deadlocks at the edge of updated regions; (3) shortcut smoothing. Cost is a weighted sum, delta*risk + distance.

Compared with the original D* Lite, nodes updated fell 34.9% in the freezing period (18,468 vs 28,351) and 79.5% in the melting period. Planning time fell 46% and 86%. Route length stayed within about 0.1%, and average risk was unchanged. Raising delta trades length for risk (freezing period: R 0.076 to 0.039, distance +3.4%). Each period is one simulated voyage, with no variance and no hardware stated. Some numbers in the text don't match the tables: 8 cells x 25 km is about 108 n mi, not 432, and the 0.07% error figure can't be reproduced.

For Paul's systems the paper is narrow. None of the router code (fec/) has D* Lite or LPA*. The gains need large graphs where repeated queries see small, local changes. The 533-node cosponsor graph is too small for incremental replanning to matter, and the staffer router serves many different origin/target pairs. Its approximate local update would also break Paul's 2026-10-03 rule that staffer routes must be exactly optimal. The paper's sharpest use is diagnostic. Its warning that extracting a path from stale cost-to-goal values can deadlock describes the dashboard's buildPath "member dropped" mode: distToTarget ignores dropped members, but tracePath skips them, so the chain labelled "PROVABLY-OPTIMAL" is not optimal once someone is dropped (UNVERIFIED, read from the code but not run). The paper also shows that scenario.py's D* Lite citation claims a reuse of earlier work that the code doesn't do.

bearings.paper_claim: If a path is extracted greedily from cost-to-goal (g) values that are out of date after cells become obstacles, it can deadlock or detour at the edge of the updated region. Their fix extracts the next node as the unexplored successor minimizing c+g, using values made consistent with the change (Sec. 2.3, Eq. 6, Algorithm 2). Without such fixes, the freezing-period run updated 28,351 nodes, against 18,468 for the improved method.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 2.3, Eq. 6, Algorithm 2, pp. 6-8; Table 3, p. 15
bearings.system_side: buildPath runs one max-product Dijkstra from the target (distToTarget). distToTarget never checks the `dropped` set (scenario-removed members). tracePath then picks successors greedily by PE*dT and skips dropped and already-seen nodes. When members are dropped, dT still counts routes through them, so the chain can be suboptimal, or come back reached=false even though a path exists. This happens under a comment that says 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL recruitment chain'. With nothing dropped, the extraction is exact.
bearings.code_ref: fec/surfaces/templates/make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:734 (distToTarget, no dropped check); :735 (PROVABLY-OPTIMAL claim); :740 (tracePath skips dropped); :753-757 (buildPath)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The mechanism is a general graph-search fact. It does not depend on ice data, so it holds for the 533-node cosponsor graph whenever the 'member out' scenario is active. The fix needed here is simpler than the paper's: at N=533, a full recompute that honors dropped costs almost nothing. The paper's own timing evidence (one voyage, no hardware stated) does not carry over. The finding is UNVERIFIED (DE-062): it comes from reading the code and has not been reproduced by running the dashboard. A related unchecked point: distToTarget propagates d[v]=d[u]*PE[u][v] outward from the target while tracePath walks PE forward, which only matches if PE is symmetric.

bearings.paper_claim: The improved local-update rule cuts nodes updated by 34.9%-79.5% and planning time by 46%-86% compared with the original D* Lite, but it is approximate. Route length differs from full re-planning by up to about 0.1% (2,558.7 vs 2,561.4 n mi freezing; 2,419.1 vs 2,418.1 melting), and no optimality guarantee is given.
bearings.system_side: The staffer router is an exact bidirectional Dijkstra (heuristic 0). Under Paul's 2026-10-03 ruling, routes whose costs fall within 1e-12 relative count as ties, broken by fewer steps. Results are cached under a key that includes the graph revision, so any revision change forces a full fresh search. The search is not reused incrementally.
bearings.code_ref: fec/surfaces/staffer_closeness_routes.py:1-21 (exact search and tie contract), :79 (ALGORITHM); fec/surfaces/staffer_routing.py:386 (heuristic 0), :567-572 (revision-keyed LRU cache)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Incremental replanning pays off when the same start and goal are re-queried after small, local edge changes on a large graph. The staffer graph is large (about 4.66M overlap pairs), but each request has a different origin and office target, and revisions arrive in batches from the identity loop. That is not one agent moving through slowly changing ice. Plain D* Lite or LPA* (which stay exact) could only fit a standing saved route that is re-checked after a revision. The paper's approximate rule would break the exact-cost ruling. ALT landmarks were already deferred by Paul (2026-10-02) and come first.

bearings.paper_claim: D* Lite-family planners save work only by reusing earlier search state and updating the nodes a change touches. The paper reports 18,468 vs 72,835 node updates compared with full re-planning (freezing) and 16,864 vs 114,929 (melting).
bearings.system_side: The scenario.py docstring cites Ren et al.'s D* Lite for 'recompute only what the scenario actually touches'. The code recomputes baseline and scenario spread for every category on every run (and flip_value for every category in fm.cat2sc). Baseline and scenario are isolated by common random numbers, not by reusing earlier work.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/scenario.py:13 (citation claim); :42-52 (CRN cascade); :103-104 and :113-115 (full per-category recompute)
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is about documentation only. At 533 members and MC=40, a full recompute is cheap, so building incremental reuse is not justified (YAGNI). The docstring should credit CRN isolation, not D* Lite reuse. The paper's numbers say nothing about the cascade itself.

bearings.paper_claim: The movement cost is a weighted sum, delta*r + d. Raising delta from 1 to 3 lowers average risk from 0.076 to 0.039 and lengthens the route by 3.4% (freezing, Icemax 1.2 m). delta=3 is picked as 'sufficient' on unpublished simulations. The authors never show a Pareto front.
bearings.system_side: The route finder sweeps lambda over {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} in value = (gain - lambda(1-p))/cost. It builds greedy routes and keeps only the non-dominated (cost, spread, risk) points. It does no shortest-path search and no incremental replanning. The MOPBD* citation is conceptual only.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/cosponsor_route.py:40-63 (greedy route with lambda risk penalty), :64-76 (Pareto filter over lambda sweep)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The two papers share only the move of putting risk into the cost as a weighted sum. The system goes further than the paper by sweeping and reporting the front instead of fixing one delta. Weighted-sum scalarization can miss non-convex front points in both. D* Lite does not plug into this greedy builder, and at 533 nodes replanning cost is not a bottleneck.

gaps_exposed: Dashboard recruitment-path 'member dropped' mode: distToTarget (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:734) ignores the dropped set, while tracePath (:740) skips dropped members. The chain labelled 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL' (:735) can then be suboptimal or falsely unreachable. The simple fix is to honor dropped in distToTarget (a full recompute is cheap at N=533). UNVERIFIED until reproduced by running the dashboard.

No incremental replanning (D* Lite or LPA*) exists anywhere in fec/ routing code; a search of fec/*.py, *.tpl and *.js found only citations. The only place it could plausibly pay off is a standing staffer route re-checked after a graph revision, and it ranks behind the deferred ALT work.
scenario.py credits D* Lite-style 'recompute only what the scenario touches', but recomputes every category. The real mechanism is CRN isolation, and the docstring should say so.

None of the system's route objectives has a sensitivity table like the paper's Table 5 (route outcome as the risk weight changes). The cosponsor Pareto sweep comes closest, but ASKM (0.07) and HOP_FACTOR are not swept.
flags: Do not port the paper's local-update rule (Eq. 5) into the staffer router. It is approximate (about 0.1% length deviation, no optimality proof) and would break Paul's 2026-10-03 ruling that route costs must match exactly, with ties at 1e-12 relative.

The dashboard optimality finding (dropped members ignored in distToTarget) is new agent analysis from reading the code. Under DE-062 it stays UNVERIFIED until a second path, such as running the dashboard with a dropped member and comparing against a Dijkstra that honors dropped, reproduces it.
scenario.py:13 overclaims: it cites D* Lite reuse that the code does not perform.

Some of the paper's numbers are unreliable: '8 grid units = 432 n mi' (should be about 108 n mi), the 0.07% error figure can't be reproduced from Tables 3-4, timings are single runs with no hardware stated, and the claim that risk is monotone in Icemax fails in the melting sweep. Quote its percentages only as single-voyage simulation results.
The paper says nothing on SNA, LDA, reciprocity or influence wording, so no brain wording rules are triggered.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul marked D* dynamic replanning 'Very interesting' and made D* Lite / LPA* the operational layer in his addendum. The paper supports the general claim: an incremental D* Lite variant re-plans with 35-86% fewer node updates than the original, at nearly the same route quality. But it shows that only on a 136k-cell grid where change is gradual and local, which doesn't fit any built router. The cosponsor graph is 533 nodes, and the staffer router serves many different origin/target pairs. The paper's approximate update rule would also break Paul's own exact-tie ruling. His note is not wrong but now ranks lower: the system has since moved to exact bidirectional Dijkstra, with ALT deferred (2026-10-02), so incremental replanning comes after ALT. The paper's most useful lesson for him is diagnostic: stale cost-to-goal values break greedy path extraction, which is what the dashboard's dropped-member mode does today.

related.why: Both papers extend D* Lite. Ren adds multiple objectives (MOPBD*). Its citations in cosponsor_route.py and scenario.py are conceptual, the same overreach this paper exposes.
Another improved D* Lite, applied to UAV firefighting. Its local-replanning changes are a close parallel to Xu's ship-routing changes.
Uses D* Lite for dynamic re-planning inside multi-agent conflict-based search. Same incremental-replanning base, multi-agent setting.
Risk-aware path objective (maximize the chance of arriving on time). It underlies the dashboard's max-product chain, where Xu's weighted-sum risk cost is the alternative way to price risk.
Survey of A*/D*-family pathfinding that puts D* Lite variants in context and is cited in Paul's pathfinding positions.
Speeds up single-source shortest paths from scratch, the opposite strategy to Xu's reuse of earlier search state.
